questions.question: Define an indicator and state the colour changes of red and blue litmus in an acid, a base and a neutral solution. Explain why both are needed.
questions.expected_answer: An indicator is a substance that changes colour depending on whether a solution is acidic, basic or neutral. Acid: blue litmus turns red, red stays red. Base: red litmus turns blue, blue stays blue. Neutral: neither changes. Both are needed because if only one colour is used and it does not change, the substance could be neutral or the other type (blue staying blue could be a base or neutral; red staying red could be an acid or neutral).

questions.question: Describe a safe and fair procedure to test six household substances with litmus, and draw up the headings of a suitable results table with two example rows.
questions.expected_answer: Wear goggles; use only approved substances; label clean containers; dissolve solids in water; use a clean or rinsed rod for each substance to avoid contamination; place drops on red and blue litmus on a white tile; observe and record immediately; keep amounts and method the same; repeat tests. Table headings: Substance | Red litmus | Blue litmus | Acid, base or neutral. Example rows: Vinegar | stays red | turns red | acid. Baking soda solution | turns blue | stays blue | base. (Sugar water | stays red | stays blue | neutral.)

questions.question: Explain how to make red cabbage indicator and state its colours in an acid, a neutral and a base. Give one advantage it has over litmus.
questions.expected_answer: Chop red cabbage, soak or gently boil it in water until the water is deep purple, then strain off the leaves. Acid (vinegar, lemon juice): pink or red. Neutral (pure water, sugar water): purple. Base (baking soda, soap): blue or green, yellow in strong bases. Advantage: it shows several colours, so it gives an idea of how strongly acidic or basic a substance is, not just which group it belongs to; it can also be made at home from food.
